1261.title: The Prophet's intercession
1261.hook: the Prophet ﷺ will intercede for his community (Bukhari)
1261.howItsDone: Muslims send blessings on the Prophet, salawat, in their prayers and when his name is mentioned, and after the call to prayer they may ask Allah to grant him al-wasilah, hoping for his intercession on the Day of Resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sirat, the bridge over the fire, crossed by the light you bring.

The plain is crowded and the waiting is long, and people do what people do when things are hard: they look for someone to speak for them. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Anas, tells it as a search. They go to Adam: will you ask your Lord for us? Not me, he says, and sends them on. To Noah. Not me. To Abraham. To Moses. To Jesus. Each one gently says: not me, go to another. And the last one sends them to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
screen: `A SEARCH ACROSS THE PLAIN.` → `ADAM, NOAH, ABRAHAM, MOSES, JESUS.` → `NOT ME. GO TO ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: The word is shafa'ah, intercession: speaking to someone on another's behalf. In the hadith, the Prophet goes, and the first thing he does is not speak. He falls down in prostration before his Lord, and stays there. Then he is told: raise your head; ask, and you will be given; intercede, and your intercession will be accepted. Then he intercedes. Two things hold this teaching in place. First, the Qur'an is clear that intercession is never a way around Allah. In the Throne Verse, Pickthall's translation asks: "Who is he that intercedeth with Him save by His leave?" Nobody speaks on the Day unless permitted; the Prophet's intercession is a permission, granted. Second, it was saved. Another hadith in Bukhari has him say that every prophet has one prayer sure to be answered, and he wanted to keep his back, as intercession for his community on the Day of Resurrection. Theologians from the part we just finished discussed who it reaches. Sunni theologians, as they're remembered, affirmed that it can reach believers who sinned gravely; the Mu'tazilah held a narrower view. The hadith also name a way to ask for it. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever sends one blessing on the Prophet, Allah sends ten on them; and that whoever, after the call to prayer, asks Allah to grant him the station called al-wasilah, his intercession becomes due for that person. So the blessing travels both ways: the community sends salawat to him, and the hope is that he speaks for them.
screen: `NOT SPEECH FIRST: PROSTRATION.` · `SAVE BY HIS LEAVE.` · `ONE PRAYER, KEPT FOR THE DAY.` · then, large: `BLESSING SENT, INTERCESSION HOPED FOR.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, say the familiar words slowly, a few times, in Arabic or in English: allahumma salli 'ala Muhammad, O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad. If you're not, sit with the shape of the idea: bring to mind someone who once spoke up for you when you couldn't speak for yourself, a parent, a teacher, a friend in a hard meeting, and wish them well.
Shafa'ah. Intercession: speaking for another, only by Allah's leave; the Prophet's, Muslims hold, kept for his community on the Day. Today's word.
Your line: he will intercede. Only by Allah's leave, and kept for the Day. Rest easy tonight.

1262.title: The Prophet's pool
1262.hook: the Prophet's pool, whiter than milk, where his community drinks
1262.carry: at the prophet's pool, thirst ends for good
1262.howItsDone: Muslims affirm the Prophet's pool (al-hawd) as part of belief in the unseen events of the Last Day, drawing on descriptions in the hadith collections; hadith-based manners include saying bismillah before drinking and sipping in a few breaths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shafa'ah, the Prophet's intercession, and your line: he will intercede. Today, a drink of water on the long Day.

Thirst is about as plain as a feeling gets. A long walk in the heat, a dry mouth, then a cup of cold water, and for a moment nothing else matters. The hadith collections describe the Day of Judgment as a long, hard standing, and into that picture they place something simple: a pool. Not a palace, not a throne. Water. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoke of it to his companions as a place where he would be waiting for them.
screen: `A DRY MOUTH, A COLD CUP.` → `A LONG STANDING.` → `AND THEN, WATER.`

segments.voice: The word is hawd, a pool or basin, a place to drink. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet describes his pool. Its water is whiter than milk. Its scent is sweeter than musk. Its cups are as many as the stars in the sky. Its size is a month's journey. And whoever drinks from it will never be thirsty again. Notice what kind of picture this is. It isn't reward measured in gold. It's thirst ending. Water is the line between life and death, and here that line is drawn for good. Other reports in Bukhari have him say he will go ahead of his people and be at the pool before them. His word is farat, and some commentators explain it as the one who rides ahead of a caravan to find water and get the buckets ready. So the picture is personal: someone who went first, waiting at the water with cups. Some reports also connect the pool to al-Kawthar, the abundance named in Surah al-Kawthar, which opens in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! We have given thee Abundance." Scholars have discussed how the river and the pool relate, and they don't all describe it the same way. Muslims hold the pool among the unseen things to be believed, without needing to know its shape. And at an ordinary kitchen sink, the teaching turns a glass of water into a reminder: every time thirst ends, the believer can recall the thirst that ends for good.
screen: `HAWD: A POOL, A PLACE TO DRINK.` · `WHITER THAN MILK, NEVER THIRSTY.` · `HE GOES AHEAD, AND WAITS.` · then, large: `EVERY GLASS, A REMINDER.`

segments.voice: Take a glass or bottle of water in your hand, or if there's none nearby, simply notice your mouth and your breath. Pause and notice the thirst, small as it is, then take a slow sip and feel it go down. Muslim table manners, taken from hadith, include saying bismillah first and sipping in a few breaths, so if you pray, say bismillah now; if not, just let the water be water, and let it end a thirst.
Hawd. A pool, a basin: the Prophet's pool on the Day, whiter than milk, where his community drinks and is never thirsty again. Today's word.
Your line: at the prophet's pool, thirst ends for good. Every glass of water can carry a little of it. See you tomorrow.

1263.title: The fire
1263.hook: described so people turn back in time
1263.howItsDone: Muslims affirm the fire as part of belief in the Last Day; some teachers present its descriptions alongside the hadith about protecting oneself even with half a date in charity, and Muslims ask Allah's forgiveness for wrongs they turn away from.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hawd, the Prophet's pool, and your line: the pool. Today, the hardest picture on this part of the path.

A sign on a mountain road: sharp bend ahead, slow down. Nobody puts it there to frighten drivers for fun. It's there because someone wants them to make the turn. The Qur'an speaks of the fire in plain, hard language, and first-time readers sometimes stop there. But the Qur'an itself says why the warning is given, and the hadith add a surprising detail about how small the way out can be.
screen: `A SIGN BEFORE THE BEND.` → `HARD LANGUAGE.` → `WHY THE WARNING?`

segments.voice: In Arabic the fire is simply an-nar, and the Qur'an gives it other names too. Muslims hold it as real, part of the unseen they believe in, alongside the pool and the garden. The descriptions are not soft. But look at the frame. In one passage, after describing the fire, the Qur'an says this is how Allah warns His servants, then turns straight to them: so be mindful of Me. The picture comes with an address, spoken to people who still have time. The Qur'an also draws a line. Forgiveness is for those who do wrong in ignorance and turn back soon, not for one who keeps doing evil until death arrives and only then says, now I repent. So the warning is about timing: turn back in time. Now the surprise. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet, peace be upon him, tells people to protect themselves from the fire, even with half a date given in charity. Not a fortune, not a lifetime of perfection. Half a piece of fruit, given to someone hungry. Another report adds: if you don't have even that, then with a kind word. The same tradition that describes the fire in hard language makes the door out very small and very near. Muslim scholars have discussed the fire's nature in detail, and they don't all agree on every question. But on the purpose of the warning, the text is clear. It's a sign before the bend.
screen: `AN-NAR: DESCRIBED IN HARD LANGUAGE.` · `A WARNING, SPOKEN TO THE LIVING.` · `TURN BACK BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE.` · then, large: `EVEN WITH HALF A DATE.`

segments.voice: Let one small wrong come to mind, something you've been doing lately and would rather stop: a sharp word, a habit, a corner you keep cutting. Without judging yourself, picture the bend in the road, and picture taking the turn: one concrete thing you'll do differently. If you pray, ask Allah's forgiveness in your own words; if not, simply hold the decision.
The fire. An-nar: described in the Qur'an in hard language, as a warning spoken to people who still have time to turn back. Today's word.
Your line: turn back in time. Even half a date can be the turn. Tomorrow, the garden.

1264.title: The garden
1264.hook: what no eye has seen or ear heard
1264.howItsDone: Muslims affirm the garden (jannah) as part of belief in the Last Day; teachers often pair the Qur'an's descriptions with the hadith qudsi that it holds what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fire, and your line: turn back in time. Today, the other side of the picture.

Try describing the color red to someone who has never seen color. You can say warm, you can say fire, you can say the inside of a pomegranate. Every word points, and none of them arrives. The Qur'an describes the garden of paradise with rivers, shade, fruit and peace. And then the tradition does something unexpected. It says, in effect: whatever you're picturing, it's more than that.
screen: `RED, TO SOMEONE WHO NEVER SAW COLOR.` → `RIVERS, SHADE, FRUIT.` → `MORE THAN THAT.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is jannah, a garden, and the Qur'an pictures it in many passages: gardens with rivers flowing beneath, shade that doesn't fade, fruit within reach, greetings of peace. Then comes a hadith qudsi, a saying the Prophet, peace be upon him, reports from Allah. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Allah says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to a human heart. Three doors, all closed. Not the eye, not the ear, not even imagination. In the same report, the companion Abu Hurayrah adds: recite, if you like, this verse. In Pickthall's translation: "No soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy, as a reward for what they used to do." Kept hid. So the Qur'an's descriptions are real, and Muslims take them seriously, but they're also signposts, pointing at a joy bigger than the pointing. Scholars have discussed how literally to read the garden's details, and they've answered in more than one way. But this hadith keeps everyone humble: whatever your picture is, it's smaller than the thing. So the garden isn't a catalog to be calculated. It's a hope that stays open, and the best joy you've tasted is a hint, not the whole.
screen: `JANNAH: A GARDEN WITH RIVERS.` · `NO EYE, NO EAR, NO HEART.` · `KEPT HID: A JOY BEYOND THE PICTURE.` · then, large: `A HINT, NOT THE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one moment of real joy, a laugh at a kitchen table, cool water on a hot day, someone's face lighting up when they saw you, and let the light and sounds fill in for a few breaths. Then hold the hadith beside it, no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and let your joy be a hint pointing past itself. If you pray, thank Allah for that moment with alhamdulillah; if not, let it be a plain thank-you.
The garden. Jannah: paradise in the Qur'an, rivers and shade and peace, and in the hadith, a joy that no eye has seen and no heart has imagined. Today's word.
Your line: no eye has seen. Whatever you picture, it's more. Go gently.

1265.title: Seeing Him
1265.hook: the believers will see their Lord as they see the moon
1265.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims (Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari) affirm that believers will see their Lord in the hereafter without asking how, citing this hadith and Qur'an 75:22–23; the Mu'tazilah and Twelver Shia theologians hold that Allah is not seen with physical eyes and read these texts differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garden, and your line: no eye has seen. Today, the hope at the center of that garden.

Night. A group of companions is sitting with the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the moon is full. The companion Jarir ibn Abdullah remembers what came next. The Prophet looked at it and spoke. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Jarir reports it: you will see your Lord as you see this moon, and you will have no trouble seeing Him. A whole crowd under one moon, and nobody pushing for a better look.
screen: `A FULL MOON, A CIRCLE OF FRIENDS.` → `HE LOOKS UP.` → `AS YOU SEE THIS MOON.`

segments.voice: Why the moon? Look at the hadith's own words: no trouble seeing Him. A full moon is one thing, and everyone sees it at once. Nobody stands in line; nobody blocks anyone's view. The comparison is about the seeing, clear and shared, not about Allah being like the moon, and Muslim teachers are careful on that point. The Qur'an speaks of the same hope. In Pickthall's translation: "That day will faces be resplendent, Looking toward their Lord." Here the theologians from earlier in this block return, because this was one of their real questions. Another verse says vision does not grasp Him, while He grasps all vision. How do the two fit? The Ash'ari and Maturidi schools, and the Athari approach, affirm that the believers will truly see their Lord in the hereafter, without asking how. The Mu'tazilah held that Allah is not seen with the eyes, and read the verses about seeing another way. Twelver Shia theology, too, holds that He is not seen with physical eyes, and speaks of a seeing of the heart. Each side reads both verses. What they share is the hope of nearness to Allah. And that gives these unseen days a direction. Not only escape from the fire or a stay in the garden, but a face turned toward its Lord.
screen: `THE MOON: CLEAR, AND SEEN BY ALL.` · `FACES LOOKING TOWARD THEIR LORD.` · `THE THEOLOGIANS READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `A FACE TURNED TOWARD ITS LORD.`

Notice how it looks the same to everyone under it, and let the hadith come to mind: as you see this moon. If you pray, hold the hope of that seeing in silence; if not, rest in the plain wonder of the light.

1266.title: Mercy's hundred parts
1266.hook: Allah made mercy in a hundred parts and sent down one
1266.howItsDone: Some Muslim teachers cite the hadith of mercy's hundred parts alongside descriptions of the Day of Judgment, so that hope and fear are held together; Muslims call on Allah as ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, the names in the bismillah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seeing Him, and your line: like seeing the moon. Today, the hadith that sits over the whole unseen journey.

A horse stands over her newborn foal in the straw. She shifts her weight, and before her hoof comes down, she lifts it, carefully, so it doesn't land on the little one. A small thing. If you've watched animals with their young, you may have seen moves like it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, pointed to exactly that moment, and said it comes from somewhere.
screen: `A MARE AND HER FOAL.` → `SHE LIFTS HER HOOF.` → `WHERE DOES THAT COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, from Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase. Allah made mercy in a hundred parts. He kept ninety-nine with Himself, and sent one part down to the earth. From that one part, all creation shows mercy to each other, so much that the mare lifts her hoof away from her foal, afraid of hurting it. In Sahih Muslim, a version adds where the ninety-nine are kept: for the Day of Resurrection, to be shown to His servants then. Sit with the arithmetic. Every kindness you've ever seen comes from one part. A parent up in the night with a sick child. A stranger who held the door. A nurse who stayed after her shift. The mare and her hoof. All of it together is a hundredth. Now look at where this lands in the path. For days we've walked the unseen: death, the grave, the gathering, the scale, the bridge, the fire. What will that Day be like? Ninety-nine parts of mercy are being kept for it. The Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall's translation: "My mercy embraceth all things." Some Muslim teachers hold the warnings and the mercy side by side, so that neither fear nor hope swallows the other. And the one part was sent down to be used. Every time someone is gentle, that part is moving through the world, and the next kind thing you do is a small piece of it.
screen: `ONE PART SENT DOWN, NINETY-NINE KEPT.` · `ALL KINDNESS ON EARTH IS ONE PART.` · `THE NINETY-NINE, KEPT FOR THAT DAY.` · then, large: `MY MERCY EMBRACETH ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who could use a little gentleness from you, maybe someone you've been short with, or someone carrying a lot. If you pray, call on Allah as ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim; if not, simply hold the person in mind with care.

1267.title: Theology close
1267.hook: belief is reasoned about, but lived in the heart
1267.tomorrow: I was sent to perfect character
1267.howItsDone: Muslims study the articles of faith and the questions of theology, and teachers also stress that faith shows in deeds; Muslims may also pray two voluntary rak'ahs outside the five daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy's hundred parts, and your line: ninety-nine kept for that day. Today the week ends, and so does this whole block on belief.

Some desert Arabs came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and announced: we believe. The Qur'an records the answer he was told to give, gentle but firm. Don't say you believe. Say you've submitted. Faith hasn't yet entered your hearts. It's a striking line to end a block of theology on. For weeks we've talked about what Muslims believe and how theologians argued about it, and here the Qur'an says belief isn't finished when you can say it. It has to go somewhere.
screen: `WE BELIEVE, THEY SAID.` → `SAY RATHER: WE SUBMIT.` → `FAITH HAS TO ENTER THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Look back at the road. The block opened with the six articles of faith: Allah the One, the angels, the books, the messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Then the theologians: kalam, the Mu'tazilah and their justice, the trial over the created Qur'an, al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi, the Athari approach, Shia theology, and the hard question of suffering. Then the unseen journey: death and return, the grave, the questions, the trumpet, the gathering, the book, the scale, the bridge, and this week, the intercession, the pool, the fire, the garden, seeing Him, and mercy in a hundred parts. The theologians argued hard, and well, and disagreed in earnest, and their work is still studied. But the verse about the desert Arabs puts it in its place. Saying it is one step. Faith entering the heart is another. A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the other half. Faith, the Prophet said, has many branches. The highest is saying there is no god but Allah. The lowest is moving something harmful out of the road. And modesty is a branch of faith too. The top branch is a creed. The bottom branch is a rock on a path, moved so nobody trips. That's the bridge to the next block. Belief is reasoned about, but lived. Starting tomorrow, the path turns inward, to character and the heart's stations: what belief looks like in a person.
screen: `SIX ARTICLES, THE THEOLOGIANS, THE UNSEEN.` · `SAYING IT IS ONE STEP.` · `FROM A CREED TO A ROCK IN THE ROAD.` · then, large: `REASONED ABOUT, BUT LIVED.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you can pray two voluntary rak'ahs now, slowly, as you've been taught, letting each movement carry what this block taught you. If you don't pray, or can't right now, sit quietly and let one belief from these weeks come to mind. Then ask one plain question: where would this show up in my hands, a hand on a door, a word to a neighbor, a rock moved off a path?
Theology close. The end of a block on belief: the articles, the theologians, the unseen journey, and a reminder that faith is reasoned about, but has to be lived. Today's word.
Your line: believe, and live it. A creed at the top, a rock moved from the road at the bottom. Tomorrow, a new block begins.
